label: House majority
question: Democrats win a House majority (218 or more of 435)
rationale: Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946, and no president under 40 percent approval has gained. Democrats need a net 3 from a 215 baseline. Redistricting nets Republicans roughly 4 to 10 seats. The median district sits about 3.4 points right of the nation (Sabato via Washington Examiner). So Democrats need a national House margin above roughly D+3.5. Markets put the median near D+8.5 to D+9. DDHQ (77) is stale by two days and weights fundamentals. Markets (90) are closer to the polling. Independence signal at lock: the Republican House super PAC abandoned two of its own incumbents three weeks out. Moved 88 to 90, the stated ceiling.
biggest_unknown: The final week's likely-voter generic ballot. Below D+4 makes this a toss-up.
counter_case: Polling error that overstates Democrats by 4 or more points, as in 2014, plus a map that converts a D+4 popular vote into fewer than 218 seats. Republicans hold the House in that world.
alternate: Republicans hold the House with 218 to 222 seats.
flip_trigger: National House popular vote margin under D+3.5 on the certified count, or a final-week LV generic ballot average under D+4 with DCCC cuts in Trump +5 to +10 seats.
indep_signal: Committee triage. CLF canceled all remaining reservations for two GOP incumbents (IA-01, NJ-07) Oct 10-11, the first incumbent cuts of the cycle, and pulled money from MI-08, OH-01 and NE-02

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
rationale: Democrats need 51 (50 plus Vance is Republican). They hold 47 with caucusing independents and must net 4. Summing our race numbers gives an expected 50.5 Democratic seats. With correlated outcomes that is close to a coin flip. DDHQ says 56. Markets say 62 to 65. The gap is our shading of red-state polls (TX, OH, AK, IA). Red-state Senate polls overstated Democrats in the 2014 and 2018 midterms and in 2020 and 2024. Markets follow those polls. We shade toward the Republican. Independence signals at lock nudged NC, GA, SC and KS. Moved 52 to 53.
biggest_unknown: Whether the Texas and Ohio polls are right this time. Those two seats decide control in most paths.

alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with TX or OH plus AK.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter polls in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state.
indep_signal: Committee triage. combined effect of the NC, GA, SC and KS signals above on the expected seat count (about +0.1 seats)

rationale: Base rate: the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms since 1946, and no president under 40 percent approval has gained. Democrats need a net 3 from a 215 baseline. flip_trigger: National House popular vote margin under D+3.5 on the certified count, or a final-week LV generic ballot average under D+4 with DCCC cuts in Trump +5 to +10 seats.

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
weakest_component: Ohio. Its polls have overstated Democrats in each of the last four cycles and Ohio has no party-coded early vote to test it.
confidence_ceiling: 0.60 in either direction. Four races within 4 poll points of even decide it.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.

counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.

label: Senate control
question: Democrats control the Senate (51+ seats with caucusing independents; 50 plus VP counts as Republican)
weakest_component: Ohio. Its polls have overstated Democrats in each of the last four cycles and Ohio has no party-coded early vote to test it.
confidence_ceiling: 0.60 in either direction. Four races within 4 poll points of even decide it.
rationale: Re-derived from zero. Democrats need 51 and hold 47 with caucusing independents. Summing this run's race numbers gives about 50.7 expected seats, against about 50.6 at the lock. Outcomes are correlated, so 50.7 is close to a coin flip with a slight Democratic lean. The Texas, Alaska and Iowa numbers rose and Ohio held, because the red-state shading is now about 2 to 2.5 points instead of 3 to 4. Reference class: red-state Senate polling error. Republicans beat the final polls in Ohio, Iowa and Texas in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 (inferred from memory of results, not retrieved this run). The miss was largest in presidential years (4 to 8 points) and smaller in the 2022 midterm (about 1 to 3). The 2022 Democratic overperformance was in swing states (PA, AZ, MI, NV), not in red states. So the lock's counter-case that 2022 polls underrated Democrats does not transfer to these four races. This run uses an expected Republican polling bias of about 2 to 2.5 points with a race-level error of about 5, down from the roughly 3 to 4 the lock implied. The reason is the early-vote evidence: Republican shares of early ballots are below 2022 in NC (20.7 vs 30.7), IA (29.4 vs 33.2) and CO (24.2 vs 29.8), so the presidential-year Republican turnout lift is not showing. That evidence is weak for the polling-error question. Composition says who has voted, not who wins, and the low-propensity voters behind past misses mostly vote on Election Day. Markets 63.5 (Kalshi) and 64.5 (Polymarket), DDHQ 56 (Oct 14 model). We stay below markets because the polls in all four pivotal red-state races lead by 3 to 4 points, which is inside one ordinary red-state miss.
biggest_unknown: Whether Texas and Ohio polls carry the usual Republican miss in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president.
counter_case: The 2018 analog cuts both ways. In a Democratic midterm under a Republican president, Beto O'Rourke beat his Texas polls while Republicans beat theirs in Indiana, Missouri and Tennessee (inferred, not retrieved). If the Texas pattern holds for Talarico and Brown, the polls are right or low, and control is near 65 as markets say.
alternate: Democrats win 51 to 53 seats with Texas or Ohio plus Alaska.
flip_trigger: Democrats lead final likely-voter averages in both Texas and Ohio by 4 or more, or NRSC/SLF cut reservations in either state. Either moves this to about 62.
